title_en: ‘Hong Kong is back’ narrative built on more than hope and hype
content_en:
The city’s recovery is grounded in rapid economic growth, strong corporate earnings, surging office leasing and increased IPO proceeds.
An electronic ticker shows stock market prices at Exchange Square in Central on July 21. Proceeds of IPOs in Hong Kong have reached US$51.9 billion this year. Photo: Jelly Tse
Hong Kong will be one of the fastest-growing economies in the Asia-Pacific this year. That is according to Goldman Sachs, which expects the city to grow 5.1 per cent.
Having contracted 3.7 per cent in 2022 and expanded just 2.6 per cent as recently as 2024, this is quite a feat. At the beginning of this year, the government anticipated growth of 2.5-3.5 per cent. Last week, it upgraded its forecast to 4.8 per cent.
In its latest report on Hong Kong’s economy in May, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) said the city has continued to reinforce its position as a global financial centre and superconnector between the Chinese mainland and the rest of the world.
Closer integration of Hong Kong with the mainland has provided a solid underpinning for the recovery. Chinese companies in the artificial intelligence (AI) supply chain have driven a boom in initial public offerings (IPOs), with listing proceeds reaching US$51.9 billion this year. This puts first-time share sales within striking distance of the record high set in 2010.
In addition to a strong technology-heavy IPO pipeline, measures to expand capital flow channels between Hong Kong and the mainland have spurred the revival of the city’s financial markets. These measures include this week’s launch by Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing of the first index to track the performance of offshore yuan bonds.
The main growth driver, however, has been exports as Hong Kong capitalises on its position as a conduit for semiconductors moving in and out of China as part of the global buildout of AI infrastructure. Nearly all the city’s memory chip shipments were re-exports, with the mainland constituting more than 80 per cent of the trade, according to Bloomberg data. Total goods exports surged more than 30 per cent in annualised terms last quarter.
Mainland Chinese buyers have also played a key role in the recovery of the housing market. According to CBRE, mainland purchasers accounted for 72 per cent of primary market transactions in the luxury market last quarter, up from 58 per cent in the second quarter. In the “super-prime” category, which covers sales of homes worth US$10 million or more, Hong Kong was the world’s most actively traded market, according to a global ranking by Knight Frank.
The view from the penthouse suite at The Arch at Kowloon Station in Hong Kong on February 3. Sales in Hong Kong’s luxury property market have been dominated by mainland buyers. Photo: Jonathan Wong
However, the two other forces influencing the city’s economy – global financial conditions and the outlook for the AI buildout – have been less supportive in recent months. Stronger-than-expected inflation in the United States has revived concerns about a steeper rise in interest rates, while a succession of shocks in the tech world have fanned fears about the financing and geopolitics of the AI boom.
Last week, US Treasury bonds suffered their sharpest weekly sell-off since US President Donald Trump launched his “Liberation Day” tariffs in April last year. Bank of America believes “a worrisome broadening of inflationary pressures” will force the US Federal Reserve to increase borrowing costs three times in the next four months.
In a report on November 16, S&P Global Ratings said “higher interest rates are back, and Hong Kong’s property markets will feel the pinch.” Secondary prices in the housing market have been more or less flat since June – in part over uncertainty around the impact of measures to stem capital outflows from the mainland – while tighter financing conditions will “continue to constrain investment demand” for commercial real estate, CBRE said.
This makes the timing of the spying scandal engulfing Nvidia, as well as the Trump administration’s tighter curbs on Chinese companies’ access to advanced AI chips the crisis was bound to trigger, particularly bad. Tech hardware stocks across Asia have been under severe strain in recent months as worries about the region’s AI-fuelled boom intensify.
[embedded media]
In a report on November 9, HSBC said Asia was acutely vulnerable to a global slowdown in AI hardware demand as “export growth beyond AI goods remains ho-hum, while investment and consumption face a multitude of headwinds across Asia”.
Even so, these threats should not obscure the bigger picture. Hong Kong’s economy and markets have been at the epicentre of global cross-currents for decades, yet the recovery in the past two years has strengthened sufficiently to allow the city to navigate headwinds without being blown off course. The “Hong Kong is back” narrative is about resilience.
Whether it is the fast pace of the economic expansion, the strong rebound in corporate earnings, the resurgence in office leasing activity led by the Central district or the increase in IPO proceeds this year to more than US$50 billion for just the third time in history, Hong Kong’s recovery is well entrenched.
While a more hawkish Fed and an increasingly uncertain outlook for the AI buildout pose risks, the city’s new-found resilience makes these threats more manageable. Having struggled to recover from a succession of domestic and external shocks, Hong Kong now faces its challenges from a position of relative strength.
By Nicholas Spiro

title_en: Anwar vows crackdown after suspicious bags at Malaysian airbase lead to US$1.2m drug bust
content_en:
The discovery has led authorities to a syndicate using military personnel and facilities to smuggle drugs to the Philippines and Indonesia.
Malaysian army personnel load supplies into a military transport plane at the Subang Air Force Base in September 2017. Drugs were discovered during a routine luggage inspection at the airbase. Photo: AP
Drugs discovered during a routine luggage inspection at a Malaysian airbase have led to the arrest of five air force personnel and the exposure of a syndicate allegedly using the military facility to smuggle methamphetamine to the Philippines and Indonesia.
The syndicate, which police believe has been operating since July, was uncovered after air force personnel at the Subang Air Force Base found five suspicious bags and a box awaiting loading into a military aircraft on Tuesday.
“The discovery was immediately reported to the Royal Malaysian Air Force Central Zone Investigation Branch, which subsequently contacted the Royal Malaysia Police’s Narcotics Criminal Investigation Department (NCID) at Bukit Aman,” Defence Minister Mohamed Khaled Nordin said in a statement on Thursday.
Police arrived on scene at 5.20pm the same day, confirmed the substances seized were dangerous drugs and arrested the five.
Khaled said this was the first such incident detected during a routine inspection. “The Ministry of Defence will not tolerate any criminal activities. Stern action will be taken against any personnel found to be involved or complicit,” he added.
Methamphetamine also known as crystal meth. The raids netted 96.64kg of suspected methamphetamine worth US$1.2 million. Photo: Shutterstock
Following the discovery, NCID director Hussein Omar Khan said police conducted a series of raids in collaboration with the air force’s Provost Marshal Branch in the Klang Valley and Labuan on Tuesday. They seized 96.64kg (213lbs) of suspected methamphetamine worth 4.83 million ringgit (US$1.2 million) and 6.98kg of liquid chemical substance. A total of 11 people were arrested and three vehicles confiscated.
Authorities estimated the seized drugs had the potential to affect around 483,000 individuals had they been successfully distributed.
“Recent developments indicate that syndicates are becoming increasingly brazen in exploiting strategic government facilities and using individuals with certain levels of access and authority to shield their criminal activities from detection by the authorities,” Hussein said in a statement.
All five air force personnel have been detained for seven days, while six other civilians are in remand for between two and five days. Preliminary drug screening found that two civilians tested positive for methamphetamine while another had a previous criminal record involving drugs.
According to initial investigations, two of the arrested civilians are believed to be the ones organising and coordinating the syndicate’s drug trafficking activities.
Police are working to uncover the syndicate’s organisational structure and identify other individuals involved. “The NCID is actively tracking another Malaysian national believed to be the syndicate’s leader,” Hussein said.
[embedded media]
The syndicate exploited the trust placed in certain individuals within the country’s security institutions, he added. “The NCID takes seriously any abuse of position, authority or official facilities for criminal purposes, as such actions not only violate the law but could also undermine institutional integrity and national security.”
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim revealed details of the syndicate during his exit press conference at the Apec meeting in Shenzhen earlier on Thursday, saying investigations were under way but police and the armed forces needed time to complete them.
“I am saying this at this press conference because I do not want anyone to think that we are deliberately delaying action,” he said as reported by local news outlet New Straits Times.
He said all those at the highest levels – including the defence and home ministers – were looking into the matter, emphasising that all parties agreed there would be no compromise in taking down the ring.
“How can we expect the country to be safe if we allow this to happen?” he said. “These are the security forces. It is like ‘harapkan pagar, pagar makan padi’,” he said. The Malay proverb about trusting the fence to guard the paddy, only for it to eat the crop, refers to how those entrusted to protect end up being the ones people need guarding against.
By Ushar Daniele

title_en: Comb restores hair growth; Kim Jong-un daughter’s luxury ski gear: SCMP’s 7 highlights
content_en:
From Chinese comb restoring hair growth to Elon Musk fuelling Hong Kong birth-rate debate, here are highlights from SCMP’s recent reporting.
Kim Ju-ae, daughter of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, skis at a tourist zone under development in Samjiyon, North Korea, on Sunday. Photo: KCNA via AP
We have selected seven stories from this week’s news across Hong Kong, mainland China, the wider Asia region and beyond that resonated with our readers and shed light on topical issues. If you would like to see more of our reporting, please consider subscribing.
1. China’s first lady Peng Liyuan lets her English do the talking in Trump welcome
Chinese first lady Peng Liyuan again let her English do the talking as she accompanied President Xi Jinping in welcoming his US counterpart Donald Trump and other leaders to Shenzhen for the Apec summit’s welcome dinner.
2. Kim Jong-un’s daughter wears European ski gear worth over a year’s pay
Kim Ju-ae, daughter of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, skis at a tourist zone under development in Samjiyon, North Korea, on Sunday. Photo: KCNA via AP
Kim Ju-ae, the daughter of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, has drawn attention after official photos of her hitting the slopes at a ski resort under development sparked speculation over the cost of her outfit.
3. Wearing briefs boosts erectile dysfunction risk, 26,000-man study in China finds
Large-scale Chinese study finds that tight briefs can affect sperm count, semen quality and sexual function. Photo: Shutterstock
A major new study out of China suggests that choosing tight underwear over classic boxer shorts could lead to higher rates of erectile dysfunction, premature ejaculation and prostatitis.
4. As foreigners in Thailand lose homes, Malaysia courts wealthy buyers
Villas under construction on a hillside in Phuket. Thai authorities have stepped up enforcement against illegal “nominee” shell companies used by foreign nationals to bypass land ownership restrictions. Photo: Shutterstock
A growing number of foreigners who thought they owned a home in Thailand are discovering they never legally did. A year-long crackdown on illegal foreign property ownership in the Southeast Asian nation has led to confiscations, arrests and prosecutions.
5. ‘Gone soon’ or ‘new blood’? Elon Musk sparks Hong Kong birth-rate debate
Tech billionaire Elon Musk has weighed in on Hong Kong’s low birth rate, saying the city’s population “will be gone soon” unless the trend reverses, but local experts and politicians have dismissed his assertion, arguing that migration will bring in “new blood”.
6. Chinese scientists’ comb restores hair growth by nearly 100% in mice study
The Detangle device developed by a research team in China. Photo: Handout
A Chinese research team developed a comb that uses microelectronics to treat hair loss.
7. China’s star bodyguard steals the show as Mexican leader arrives for Apec
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum boards a state limousine after arriving for the 33rd Apec Economic Leaders’ Meeting, in Shenzhen on November 16. Photo: CCTV
China’s most recognisable female bodyguard returned to the spotlight on Monday, following closely behind Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum as she arrived in Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.
By SCMP

title_en: Why the ball is in Kim Jong-un’s court on a meeting with Donald Trump
content_en:
North Korean leader did not make an appearance in Shenzhen for Apec and for now ‘does not see value’ in meeting US president, analyst says.
Donald Trump and Kim Jong-un shake hands before their summit in Hanoi, Vietnam in February 2019. Photo: Reuters
North Korean leader Kim Jong-un’s absence from the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation gathering in Shenzhen could indicate that a meeting with Donald Trump will not take place in the foreseeable future.
Analysts said it was a vastly different geopolitical and logistical situation from Trump’s first term, when the two leaders met three times.
Sydney Seiler, senior adviser to the Korea chair at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies, said Kim was trying to “lock in” his nuclear weapons state status and get the world to forget about denuclearisation and sanctions.
“Right now, he does not need to meet Donald Trump. He does not see value in that. Things are developing well with both China and Russia,” Seiler said during an online event hosted by the Washington-based think tank on Thursday.
During Trump’s first term, he and Kim held a summit in Singapore in June 2018, followed by a second one in Hanoi, Vietnam in February 2019. They also had an unplanned meeting at the demilitarised zone that divides the two Koreas in June 2019, while the US president was visiting South Korea.
[embedded media]
Speaking to reporters on Monday as he left the White House en route to the Philippines and China, Trump said he “may meet” Kim. At that stage he was already scheduled to join trilateral talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian leader Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Apec summit – a meeting that went ahead on Thursday and produced a “joint declaration of peace” that called for nuclear arms control.
The US leader has repeatedly expressed interest in holding another summit with Kim in his second term, while also frequently referring to North Korea as a nuclear power, in contradiction to Washington’s stance of denuclearising the Korean peninsula.
Pyongyang has demanded recognition of its nuclear state status as a prerequisite for resuming dialogue with Washington.
But Kim did not accede to Trump’s invitation for a meeting on the sidelines of Apec, with his last known activity being an inspection of a newly built ski resort near the Chinese border with his daughter Kim Ju-ae.
Kim Jong-un inspects a cable car stop at the top of Mount Paektu in Samjiyon, North Korea on Tuesday. Photo: YNA/dpa
Analysts said Kim may have seen the meeting with Trump as a logistical challenge and unnecessary, as Pyongyang strengthens its military and economic ties with Beijing and Moscow, effectively evading the sanctions Washington used as a trading card in denuclearisation talks during Trump’s first term.
Andrew Yeo, a senior fellow and the SK-Korea Foundation chair at the Brookings Institution in Washington, said Kim was “specifically meeting Trump” in 2019, while his trip to Shenzhen would have put him in the middle of the Apec summit and the “historic” meeting between Trump, Xi and Putin.
He said Kim could be trying to find the right time to meet Trump, and he might have questioned “whether he would be treated as an equal in Shenzhen, or if he would be the sideshow in a party among great-power leaders”.
“Logistically, Beijing may not have been interested in trying to orchestrate and host a Trump-Kim meeting on top of other diplomatic meetings,” Yeo said.
“Also, the preparation for Kim to attend would have had to have taken place possibly weeks in advance since Kim usually travels by train – or possibly provide an aircraft for Kim as it did in 2018 to fly to Singapore.”
Kim’s last known international flight was in June 2018, when he travelled to Singapore for the summit with Trump on a commercial Boeing 747 provided by Air China.
Since then, he has only been seen taking trains to attend meetings with foreign leaders, such as a trip to Hanoi in 2019 that took more than 60 hours and his meeting with Putin in the Russian Far East in 2023.
Victor Cha, president of the Geopolitics and Foreign Policy Department and Korea chair at the CSIS, said Kim’s absence “speaks to how he feels like he doesn’t need the meeting” despite Trump sending an “open invitation” with no conditions.
“I don’t think President Trump has put more personal face into a foreign policy issue than he has on North Korea,” Cha said during the CSIS event.
“He has said only good things about Kim, despite all the bad things that they’re doing, and Kim just decided not to show up.”
Troy Stangarone, a visiting senior fellow at the Korea Economic Institute of America, said Trump had a “fundamental misunderstanding” of Kim, pointing to the US president relegating any meeting with the North Korean leader to a “secondary affair” during the recent Apec summits.
“A meeting at this year’s Apec, for example, would have been overshadowed by the US-China-Russia trilateral meeting. The circumstances matter and North Korea has shown little interest in being a secondary meeting for Trump,” Stangarone said.
The 2019 Hanoi summit did not result in any deals and instead prompted a freeze on official US-North Korea denuclearisation discussions. Since then, North Korea has significantly expanded its nuclear and missile capabilities, from intercontinental ballistic missiles to drone fleets, and strengthened ⁠ties with Russia and China.
Donald Trump meets Kim Jong-un at the demilitarised zone separating the two Koreas in Panmunjom in June 2019. Photo: Reuters
Beijing has meanwhile been shoring up its ties with Pyongyang. Xi visited Pyongyang in June for the first time since 2019, and a new bridge across the Yalu River connecting the two countries opened last month after more than a decade of delays.
North Korea has also sent about 14,000 to 15,000 troops to support Russia’s war in Ukraine since 2024, according to Ukrainian and South Korean estimates. In exchange, Pyongyang received military technology and economic aid from Moscow.
Kim’s day trip to Dandong for a ceremony to open the Yalu River bridge in October was seen as a sign there could be a meeting ahead with Trump, since their previous summits have always been preceded by Kim visiting China.
A North Korean delegation headed by Kim’s closest ally Jo Yong-won, secretary of the ruling Workers’ Party of Korea, also met Putin at the Kremlin in Moscow just days before the Apec summit.
But Seiler said these signals were likely aimed at sending a “no” message to the invitation to meet Trump, while also showing that Beijing and Moscow had limits on their leverage to push Pyongyang to meet in China.
“In the way they handled themselves prior to Apec, both Beijing and Moscow looked like they favoured a dialogue between Donald Trump and Kim Jong-un, if it should come to fruition, but neither of them looked like they were putting much at stake,” Seiler said.
“Donald Trump, on the other hand, might feel increasingly frustrated that his overtures to Kim go ignored.”

title_display: Why the ball is in Kim Jong-un’s court on a meeting with Donald Trump
content_display:
North Korean leader did not make an appearance in Shenzhen for Apec and for now ‘does not see value’ in meeting US president, analyst says.
Donald Trump and Kim Jong-un shake hands before their summit in Hanoi, Vietnam in February 2019. Photo: Reuters
North Korean leader Kim Jong-un’s absence from the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation gathering in Shenzhen could indicate that a meeting with Donald Trump will not take place in the foreseeable future.
Analysts said it was a vastly different geopolitical and logistical situation from Trump’s first term, when the two leaders met three times.
Sydney Seiler, senior adviser to the Korea chair at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies, said Kim was trying to “lock in” his nuclear weapons state status and get the world to forget about denuclearisation and sanctions.
“Right now, he does not need to meet Donald Trump. He does not see value in that. Things are developing well with both China and Russia,” Seiler said during an online event hosted by the Washington-based think tank on Thursday.
During Trump’s first term, he and Kim held a summit in Singapore in June 2018, followed by a second one in Hanoi, Vietnam in February 2019. They also had an unplanned meeting at the demilitarised zone that divides the two Koreas in June 2019, while the US president was visiting South Korea.

Speaking to reporters on Monday as he left the White House en route to the Philippines and China, Trump said he “may meet” Kim. At that stage he was already scheduled to join trilateral talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian leader Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Apec summit – a meeting that went ahead on Thursday and produced a “joint declaration of peace” that called for nuclear arms control.
The US leader has repeatedly expressed interest in holding another summit with Kim in his second term, while also frequently referring to North Korea as a nuclear power, in contradiction to Washington’s stance of denuclearising the Korean peninsula.
Pyongyang has demanded recognition of its nuclear state status as a prerequisite for resuming dialogue with Washington.
But Kim did not accede to Trump’s invitation for a meeting on the sidelines of Apec, with his last known activity being an inspection of a newly built ski resort near the Chinese border with his daughter Kim Ju-ae.
Kim Jong-un inspects a cable car stop at the top of Mount Paektu in Samjiyon, North Korea on Tuesday. Photo: YNA/dpa

He said Kim could be trying to find the right time to meet Trump, and he might have questioned “whether he would be treated as an equal in Shenzhen, or if he would be the sideshow in a party among great-power leaders”.
“Logistically, Beijing may not have been interested in trying to orchestrate and host a Trump-Kim meeting on top of other diplomatic meetings,” Yeo said.
“Also, the preparation for Kim to attend would have had to have taken place possibly weeks in advance since Kim usually travels by train – or possibly provide an aircraft for Kim as it did in 2018 to fly to Singapore.”
Kim’s last known international flight was in June 2018, when he travelled to Singapore for the summit with Trump on a commercial Boeing 747 provided by Air China.
Since then, he has only been seen taking trains to attend meetings with foreign leaders, such as a trip to Hanoi in 2019 that took more than 60 hours and his meeting with Putin in the Russian Far East in 2023.

“A meeting at this year’s Apec, for example, would have been overshadowed by the US-China-Russia trilateral meeting. The circumstances matter and North Korea has shown little interest in being a secondary meeting for Trump,” Stangarone said.
The 2019 Hanoi summit did not result in any deals and instead prompted a freeze on official US-North Korea denuclearisation discussions. title_en: Debate erupts over China university’s US$4.6m smart system tracking ‘head-raising rates’
content_en:
An expert criticises the system as ‘formalism’, saying forced attention will not fix dull classes.
A top Chinese university has sparked concern from students and the public over its new smart classrooms — a camera setup designed to track attendance, late arrivals, and student attention. Photo: Getty Images
An elite university in eastern China has spent more than 30 million yuan (US$4.6 million) installing a smart classroom system to track students’ “head-raising rate” – an indicator intended to reflect their attentiveness during lectures – and link it to their academic scores.
Nanjing University, in Jiangsu province, came under fire after some students shared on social media that the smart system would go into operation in the first week of November, Haibao News reported.
The system, which has multiple cameras installed in each classroom, tracks attendance, tardiness and students’ head-raising rates.
Students were told by their teachers that the data collected would affect their assessment scores, and that those who performed poorly in class could even lose their eligibility to sit exams.
Using multiple cameras in each classroom, the system tracks attendance, tardiness, and students’ head-raising rates. Photo: Sohu
The system was installed in 113 classrooms during the summer holiday. The project, which cost 31.52 million yuan (US$4.7 million), includes facial checking and recognition, people counting, and the tracking of head-raising rates, according to its tender document.
The news drew significant attention online in China, as Nanjing University is among the country’s top 10 higher education institutions.
Students’ concerns and dissatisfaction grew, with some saying they feared their privacy would be infringed and their facial data collected by the university and the technology company involved.
Amid intense public pressure, the university said in a statement on November 4 that the smart classroom system would not be used to track head-raising rates, as teaching and learning methods in today’s classrooms are diverse.
The university also pledged that, without authorisation, the system would not collect biometric data or recognise faces.
Following intense public pressure and student concerns, the university pledged that the system would not collect biometric data or recognise faces without authorisation. Photo: Shutterstock
Xing Bingqi, director of the 21st Century Education Research Institute, said that even if students raised their heads in class, it did not necessarily mean they were following the lecturer’s line of thought.
“If the lecture content is not engaging and the school uses high technology to force students to raise their heads and listen, or to sit in the front rows, it will not actually improve teaching outcomes,” Xing said.
“It is simply formalism in management,” he added.
Nanjing University is not the first Chinese university to install a smart system to supervise and monitor classroom activities.
In 2024, Hangzhou Normal University in eastern China’s Zhejiang province installed a classroom-monitoring platform to capture and analyse information about classroom interactions.
While the university claims the smart system tracks students’ attentiveness, it overlooks the reality that classroom interactions are inevitable. Photo: Getty Images
China University of Mining and Technology in Jiangsu province said last year that its smart classroom platform could not only track attendance and analyse students’ “classroom status”, but also transcribe speech in real time and identify sensitive words.
A report published in June by the education news portal cernet.edu.cn said a teacher at an unnamed Chinese university received a poor teaching assessment after the classroom AI system recorded students lowering their heads to use their phones a combined 300 times.
It turned out that the students had been checking materials on their devices to prepare for group discussions.
One student in the class was labelled as having an “attention disorder” after being filmed with his head lowered throughout the lesson. In fact, he had been taking notes.
By Alice Yan

title_en: White House fires cyber chief after tech chaos rattles US
content_en:
Dismissal of Sean Cairncross is the Trump administration’s first major personnel move since recent outages.
A departures board showing cancelled flights at Logan International Airport in Boston following recent US travel disruptions. Photo: Reuters
⁠White House national cyber director Sean ⁠Cairncross was “fired” from his job, a person close to the White House said on Thursday, days after technology outages disrupted US air travel, banking and national security systems.
The ousting comes as US President Donald Trump ‌and his administration face mounting scrutiny over their response to the series of disruptions over the past week, including a global outage affecting hundreds of millions of Microsoft users and a nationwide halt to air travel that disrupted more than 18,000 flights.
The dismissal of Cairncross is the administration’s first major personnel move ⁠since the outages.
Cairncross oversaw cybersecurity policy and strategy across the federal government. Department of ‌Defense Chief Information Officer Kirsten Davies will assume the position temporarily, according to the source.
“The president fully supported firing Sean Cairncross from his ‌position,” said the person, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
Cairncross said in a ⁠statement on Thursday ⁠night it was the “honour of a lifetime to serve” in Trump’s administration.
Sean Cairncross (left) in the Oval Office in June. Photo: Reuters
The recent technology disruptions are ‌likely linked to corporate efforts to rapidly patch newly discovered software vulnerabilities in the AI age, cybersecurity experts told Reuters. ‌Advanced ‌AI tools make it easier for companies to uncover weaknesses in their cybersecurity ‌protections.
The top US intelligence official said on Wednesday the disruptions were separate service outages ⁠associated with maintenance and technical changes and not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.
Republican Senator Josh ⁠Hawley of Missouri on Tuesday told reporters in Washington the Trump administration should brief lawmakers on the outages so they can “share with the American people what’s ‌happening here”.
Cairncross was an ‌executive at the Republican National Committee before assuming the cyber director role. His successor will need to be confirmed by the US Senate, which will be controlled by Democrats beginning in January.
By Reuters

title_en: Malaysia’s military eyes gamers for South China Sea drone surveillance
content_en:
Military chief Malek Razak seeks youth digital skills to boost drone operations and modern defence capabilities.
Malaysia’s military is seeking youth digital skills, including gamers, to boost its drone operations. Photo: Shutterstock
Malaysia’s military chief Malek Razak Sulaiman said the armed forces are looking at tapping into the digital skills of the nation’s youth, including gamers, to strengthen its drone capabilities.
Malek Razak stressed, however, that experience in video games alone would not qualify someone to become a military drone operator.
Malek Razak said the military is continuously monitoring developments in defence technology and identifying the expertise required to support the operation of unmanned aerial systems, particularly for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance missions in the South China Sea.
“The increasing sophistication of military technology requires specialised knowledge and skills, including technical expertise, operational coordination and the ability to make sound decisions under challenging conditions,” he said in an interview recently.
Malaysia bought three ANKA-S units for 423.8 million ringgit (US$103 million) earlier this year and plans to buy three more in a second phase as it expands its intelligence gathering and unmanned surveillance capabilities in the South China Sea and waters off Sabah.
While experience in video games or recreational drone operations could be considered an added advantage, Malek Razak said these did not automatically translate into the competencies required for military operations.
“Operating military drones involves specialised training, technical knowledge, an understanding of operational procedures, discipline and the ability to carry out missions safely.
“An individual must possess comprehensive knowledge of the system, understand flight safety, risk management, operational procedures and responsibilities when carrying out missions,” he said.
Recruitment and selection would continue to be based on established qualifications, aptitude and competency assessments, he added.
“Digital technology and changing interests among the younger generation had created opportunities to identify potential talent for the military,” he said.
[embedded media]
Malek Razak said the military was open to exploring creative and innovative approaches to attract young Malaysians, including the use of digital platforms, interactive technology, simulations and activities based on skills.
“These could serve as effective platforms to introduce military capabilities, including unmanned systems, communications, cybersecurity and modern defence technology.
“However, such approaches must not compromise the ­standards of discipline, professionalism and responsibility expected of military personnel,” he said.
On recruitment, Malek Razak said the military was continuously reviewing its intake policies to ensure that personnel development remains relevant to technological advancements and changing security requirements.
“The expansion of Skim Perkhidmatan Askar Lasykar Angkatan Tetap (Permanent Commissioned Officers Scheme) from January 1 this year had widened academic and career opportunities for eligible personnel.
“The initiative included broader access to Skim Tauliah Pegawai Tetap (Regular Commissioned Officers Scheme) and the Special Service List category,” he said.
The armed forces had also opened recruitment opportunities to holders of vocational education and training qualifications, including the Malaysian skills certificate and Malaysian skills diploma (levels 2 and 3), as well as qualifications from the national dual training system, he added.
“The move would help broaden the recruitment pool, particularly among young people with relevant technical skills,” he said.

title_en: Russian barrage damages embassies and cathedral in Ukraine capital
content_en:
Daytime attack blows out windows at the Austrian and Dutch missions and prompts Brussels to summon Moscow’s envoy.
An employee stands behind a shattered window at the Austrian embassy in central Kyiv after a Russian drone attack. Photo: Reuters
A wave of daytime Russian strikes on Kyiv on Thursday killed one person and damaged a historic cathedral as well as the embassies of Austria and the Netherlands.
Loud explosions erupted across the Ukrainian capital throughout the day as the leaders of Russia, China and the United States held a historic meeting in China that put Russia’s President Vladimir Putin in the international spotlight.
“Russia has been terrorising Kyiv with drones all day … At least four people are known to be injured so far, and one person was killed,” Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky said.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the European Union would summon Russia’s representative in Brussels in response to the attacks, which damaged missions of both European and non-European countries.
“As Putin walked the red carpet in Shenzhen, Russian strikes hit Kyiv and damage several European and non-European embassies,” Kallas said, adding that the bloc would step up support for Ukraine and increase pressure on Moscow to end its war.
“Diplomatic premises are protected under international law. Russia’s contempt for it is on display every day,” she said.
Smoke from a Russian drone over the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Kyiv. Photo: X account of Andriy Sybiha via AFP
Images posted online by Ukraine’s foreign ministry showed the blown-out windows of the Austrian embassy.
Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker said he was shocked by the “completely unacceptable” strikes.
“The explosion happened at about 4.30pm during opening hours,” Daniel Roethlin, the embassy’s charge d’affaires, told reporters.
At the time, about 10 people were inside, he said. “Suddenly we heard the explosion, then the sirens, and we saw the smoke.”
There were no injuries but windows and vehicles were damaged, he said.
There was also damage to the nearby Saint Volodymyr Cathedral, with one of its large windows shattered and workers clearing away glass.
A fallen window frame and shattered glass inside Saint Volodymyr Cathedral after a Russian drone attack on Kyiv. Photo: Reuters
Russian strikes repeatedly targeted Kyiv’s central Podil district, from where plumes of smoke were seen rising.
The Dutch embassy was also affected, Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen said on X.
“Fortunately, our colleagues are safe and sound, although the building sustained minor damage,” he said.

title_en: Financial Street Securities says chairman detained and under investigation on mainland
content_en:
Investigation comes as Beijing continues a years-long anti-corruption campaign targeting the financial sector.
The headquarters of the China Securities Regulatory Commission in Beijing’s Xicheng district. Photo: CFOTO/Future Publishing via Getty Images
Hong Kong-listed mainland China brokerage Financial Street Securities says its chairman, Zhu Yanhui, has been placed under investigation and detained by mainland authorities in the latest case involving a senior financial executive amid a sweeping anti-corruption campaign.
Zhu was being investigated and had been subjected to detention measures, it said in a filing to the Hong Kong stock exchange on Friday that cited a notice issued by the supervisory commission in Beijing’s Xicheng district.
Zhu, 51, has served as chairman and executive director of the company since December 2022. He also chairs the company’s strategy and investment decision-making committee and its risk control and supervision committee.
Financial Street Securities’ board, excluding Zhu, said in the filing that it did not expect the investigation to have “a material impact” on its business and operations. Other directors and senior executives continued to perform their duties as normal, it said in the filing.
The company, formerly known as Hengtou Securities, came under the control of Beijing Financial Street Investment Group in 2023.
The investigation comes as Beijing continues a years-long anti-corruption campaign targeting the financial sector, with several senior securities regulators and financial executives coming under scrutiny.
In September, the authorities disclosed that Yi Huiman, former chairman of the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC), had been formally prosecuted on charges involving the acceptance of substantial bribes and abusing his position to help others in areas including listing approvals and loan arrangements.
In July, Fang Xinghai, a former CSRC vice-chairman, was placed under investigation for suspected serious violations of Communist Party discipline and the law.
At least seven securities brokerage executives have been placed under investigation by disciplinary authorities this year, including senior executives at Southwest Securities and Dongguan Securities, according to Chinese financial data provider Wind.

title_en: Hong Kong Baptist University academics create trustworthy AI-driven digital networks
content_en:
Research by Professors Xu Jianliang and Han Bo aims to ensure future computing systems are reliable and can safeguard user privacy.
Professors Xu Jianliang (left) and Han Bo, of Hong Kong Baptist University’s department of computer science, are working to enhance the trustworthiness and reliability of AI data systems.
Two Hong Kong-based computer scientists are helping to develop next-generation artificial intelligence (AI)-powered digital systems that are not only efficient and effective to use, but also – just as importantly – help to protect the privacy of users.
Professors Xu Jianliang and Han Bo are carrying out their research at Hong Kong Baptist University (HKBU) and addressing the challenge from different perspectives within their field.
“My research focuses on the foundational layer – managing, verifying and securing the data itself,” says Xu, chair professor and head of the university’s department of computer science, who joined HKBU in 2002.
“I work on database systems, privacy-preserving computing and blockchain technology to keep sensitive information confidential, yet searchable and tamper-resistant across decentralised networks.
“A long-standing challenge in our field is the trade-off between privacy protection and processing performance: stronger protection often makes data harder and slower to query.
“To address this challenge, my team is developing novel, secure indexing techniques and lightweight verification schemes. These enable systems to query data efficiently and verify its authenticity at scale without exposing the underlying raw data.”
Xu is leading two major initiatives funded by Hong Kong’s Research Grants Council (RGC), which both aim to enhance privacy protection function and the reliability of AI-powered systems.
One is centred on the private high-dimensional similarity search for cloud-based retrieval augmented generation, which helps to encrypt or obfuscate raw text; the other involves trustworthy large language models that use a multifaceted strategy for truthfulness, fairness and privacy preservation.
Last year, Xu was elected a fellow of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) – a global professional association focused on advancing technology.
He says that the IEEE’s recognition reflects his and his team’s sustained contributions to data management and privacy-preserving systems, where data integrity and confidentiality are essential.
The major turning point in his research came in 2020, during the Covid-19 pandemic, when the team developed BU-Trace – the city’s first contact-tracing system built on a strict privacy-first principle. “We wanted to demonstrate that protecting public health need not compromise personal data privacy,” he says.
They designed a decentralised solution using privacy-preserving identifiers and smartphone sensors to record venue visits and automate checkouts locally on each user’s device, without the data being uploaded onto central servers or for use by satellite-based GPS tracking.
Professor Xu Jianliang says one major problem with strong data privacy protection is that it often affects processing performance, which makes it harder and slower to query data.
The city’s government used the team’s privacy-preserving architecture for its official LeaveHomeSafe app – downloaded more than 9.5 million times up to December 2022 – and integrated its AI-powered checkout function, which had an accuracy of more than 90 per cent, along with its daily real-time “hotspot” maps.
“This work opened new possibilities for high-stakes applications that balance operational needs with personal privacy,” Xu says. “We are applying this privacy technology to support cross-border data analytics, enabling useful insights without unnecessary disclosure of sensitive personal information. Together, these efforts demonstrate how our theoretical research can help address urgent societal challenges.
“Over the next five years, I foresee computer science moving increasingly towards verifiable, privacy-preserving data architectures. AI systems rely on vast quantities of sensitive enterprise and personal data. The central challenge is no longer simply processing throughput; it is also verifying data provenance, authenticity and ownership without compromising confidentiality.”
Han – an associate professor also based at HKBU’s department of computer science – specialises in work focused on trustworthy machine learning.
Earlier this year, he was recognised by the RGC Research Fellow Scheme and secured more than HK$5.6 million (US$660,000) in funding over the next five years. This will help him build a trustworthy and efficient reasoning framework for next-generation AI agents – autonomous software programs that can perceive their environment, make independent decisions and use tools or external systems to achieve multi-step goals.
In recent years, Han has been ranked on the “World’s Top 2% Scientists” list, compiled by Stanford University in the United States. He is also a distinguished speaker for the Association of Computing Machinery, a senior member of the IEEE, and was one of the winners of the IEEE “AI’s 10 to Watch” award in 2024 and the IEEE “Computer Society’s Top 30 Early Career Professionals” award last year.
“My research operates at the intelligence layer – making sure the AI models built on top of that data remain reliable and safe,” Han says. “In the real world, data is rarely pristine. It is often noisy, corrupted, biased, or even maliciously manipulated.
“The major bottleneck we face with deep-learning models is that they tend to blindly memorise noisy data and make catastrophic errors in high-stakes settings.”
He says his team designs noise-tolerant loss functions – specialised mathematical objectives for machine learning – and cooperative learning paradigms, involving computer-based group learning, to effectively train these models, even when the training labels added to data contain errors, corruption, or noise.
“By teaching neural networks [computer systems that mimic the human brain] to filter out contaminated signals and self-correct during training, we ensure that AI remains dependable even in unpredictable, chaotic environments,” Han says.
Solving foundational reliability issues in AI cannot be done with quick, short-term workarounds,” Han says. “This sustained backing from the RGC gives my team the dedicated, uninterrupted focus needed to develop fundamentally resilient AI frameworks and address pressing issues like model hallucination, safety attacks and robustness in foundation models.”
Professor Han Bo says generative AI learning models will be widely used in areas such as medical diagnostics and finance once they are proved to be reliable.
Han believes that within a few years, generative AI models and large language models will be equipped with intrinsic self-verification and reasoning capabilities so they will eventually be able to protect themselves from vulnerability to contaminated data. Once they are proven to be reliable, they will be more widely adopted in mission-critical areas such as medical diagnostics and finance.
Both professors say that HKBU’s openness to cross-disciplinary research collaboration, combined with Hong Kong’s vibrant technology ecosystem and strategic position within southern China’s Greater Bay Area development zone, have provided them with ample resources and opportunities to continue innovating.
Xu says: “As Hong Kong strengthens its position as an international innovation and technology hub, supported by robust intellectual property protection and data standards, HKBU provides an ideal environment for translating our technological breakthroughs into meaningful, lasting societal value.”

title_en: Ex-Singapore police officer jailed for molesting intoxicated woman at hotel room
content_en:
Mohamad Joppri Harpawi forcibly kissed the victim while his cousin sexually assaulted her in 2024.
Singapore’s skyline. A former police officer was jailed for molesting a woman in the city state. Photo: Reuters
While his cousin sexually assaulted a then 25-year-old woman, a former Singapore Police Force (SPF) station inspector kissed the woman without her consent.
On Thursday, Mohamad Joppri Harpawi, 44, pleaded guilty to one count of molestation. He was sentenced to four months’ jail.
The victim cannot be named due to a gag order.
SPF said that it initiated investigations against Joppri upon establishing his involvement in the case. He was immediately removed from frontline duties and later resigned on February 11, 2025.
SPF said that its officers are expected to uphold the law and maintain the highest standards of conduct and integrity.
“We deal sternly with officers who break the law, including charging them in court,” police said.
The Attorney General’s Chambers has been contacted about whether Joppri’s cousin, 33-year-old Syafiq Hadi Surian, has been charged or sentenced over his involvement in the case.
The court heard that at about 2am on March 17, 2024, the victim and her friend were at Avenue Lounge in Marina Bay Sands when they met Joppri, Syafiq and a friend.
Joppri invited the victim and her friend to drink with them at the club. The victim became so intoxicated that she could barely walk.
Sometime after 4.45am, the men’s friend led the victim out of the club, accompanied by Joppri and Syafiq, and they left the area in a delivery van. She was told that they would be going to eat supper and she drifted in and out of consciousness.
During this time, the victim’s friend repeatedly tried to contact her, unaware she had left the club with the three men.
At some point before or during the drive, Syafiq told Joppri that he wanted to have a threesome with the victim and their male friend. Joppri then told their friend to “make sure to ask them” first, and added that he needed to be home to wake his children up for a predawn meal.
Syafiq told Joppri that the victim and their male friend were “OK” with the sexual act. However, the court heard that Syafiq never asked the victim for consent for any sexual activity.
As Joppri fell asleep, Syafiq drove the van to a hotel in Geylang. When Joppri woke up and asked why they were at a hotel, Syafiq told Joppri that he was too drunk and unable to drive any further.
At 5.16am, the group checked into two rooms. The victim and the men’s friend entered one room, while Syafiq and Joppri entered the other room.
In the room, Syafiq said he would visit the victim’s room and that “if everything was good”, the accused could enter too.
“The accused understood this term to refer to the co-accused engaging in sexual activity with the victim,” according to court documents.
The court heard that when the victim entered her room, she lost consciousness on the bed while the men’s friend lay beside her.
Syafiq entered the victim’s room first and performed a sexual act on her, which woke her up.
Joppri entered the room shortly after at Syafiq’s invitation. He then kissed the victim as she lay on the bed.
The victim pushed him away, struggled to move away from both men and told them to stop multiple times.
At about 5.26am, Joppri told Syafiq to leave the room and both men left.
Joppri later texted the victim’s friend and asked where she was and if they could meet up. He did not mention the victim nor that they were together at the hotel in Geylang.
At about 6.07am, the victim sent messages to her friend to ask for help and say that she had been touched by the two men. Her friend then called the police and the two men were apprehended the same day.
Deputy public prosecutors Selene Yap, Timothy Ong and Clara Low sought a sentence of three and a half to five months’ jail.
The prosecution noted there was skin-to-skin contact between Joppri and the victim and that the victim was vulnerable as she was intoxicated.
“Although the accused did not intrude on a private part, his act of forcibly kissing the victim on her lips is nonetheless an act that has clear sexual overtones, and accordingly has some degree of sexual exploitation,” the prosecution said.
In his mitigation plea, Joppri said his divorce was finalised 11 days before the offence and he was facing bankruptcy proceedings. He sought a sentence of six weeks’ jail.
Joppri also has five children, including a son with autism. The court also heard that he had been diagnosed with severe alcohol use disorder and moderate major depressive disorder, which had a “limited contributory link” to the offence.
He was represented by Kanthan Raghavendra, Shaneet Nityanand Rai, Kalidass Murugaiyan and Yip Jian Yang of Kalidass Law Corporation.
On the morning of the court hearing, Joppri voluntarily transferred S$500 (US$387) to the victim. Taking this into account, the prosecution sought a further S$1,000 in compensation.
However, Joppri’s lawyers said that Joppri had borrowed the money from a friend, was unemployed and was financially dependent on his partner.
Taking into account the payment and Joppri’s financial circumstances, the judge did not order further compensation.
Anyone found guilty of outrage of modesty faces up to three years’ jail, caning, a fine or any combination of the three punishments.

title_en: As Shenzhen’s ‘wonders’ dazzle Apec, what can Hong Kong offer global businesses?
content_en:
Hong Kong’s largest-ever delegation promotes city’s financial edge, Northern Metropolis and Greater Bay Area ties.
Hong Kong's leader John Lee addresses the CEO Summit on November 17. Photo: Sam Tsang
As Shenzhen presents its “wonders” to more than 2,000 business leaders, politicians and media representatives gathered for Apec meetings, Hong Kong has seized the opportunity to highlight its prowess as an international financial hub and its broader strengths.
Beyond litter-free streets flanked by crowded skyscrapers and neatly arranged, colourful landscaping, the mainland Chinese city has been awash with Apec slogans reading “Gather in Shenzhen, witness the wonders” during this week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation CEO Summit and leaders’ meeting.
Hong Kong capitalised on the events by sending its largest-ever delegation of 54 members to the CEO Summit, where they engaged with global business leaders and gained first-hand insights from their counterparts.
“Many foreign leaders have not seen what Shenzhen looked like before and see today’s Shenzhen,” Trade Development Council chairman Frederick Ma Si-hang told the South China Morning Post after attending the summit.
“Hong Kong has contributed a lot to Shenzhen over the past 40 years or so, and is still contributing to its development, albeit in other forms.
“It is truly a tale of two cities.”
Shenzhen displays Apec banners and is resplendent with floral displays for the 33rd Economic Leaders’ Meeting. Photo: Sam Tsang
Once a rural farmland backwater, Shenzhen last year overtook Shanghai and Beijing to become the nation’s largest manufacturing and exporting city while solidifying its lead in artificial intelligence (AI) and start-up cultivation.
It is home to drone-maker DJI, tech giant Tencent, telecoms firm Huawei Technologies and electric-vehicle maker BYD.
The Apec meetings were not only a high-level networking occasion; they were also used to highlight Shenzhen’s technological achievements. Shows and visits were arranged for global media to witness wonders including a robot dance performance and tours of the Longgang Energy Ecology Park and the robot block in the same district, where the latest inventions were on display.
“China’s 15th five-year plan provides a clear road map to all potential investors of the country’s goals as reflected in the host location of Shenzhen, a city that has transformed into a thriving technopole in the past decades,” Philip Kadoorie, vice-chairman of Hong Kong energy giant CLP Holdings, said after attending the CEO Summit.
“China continues to provide clear leadership, powerful incentives and a predictable environment for foreign investment in China and the Asia-Pacific.”
Robots serve in the dining area of the media centre at the Shenzhen Convention and Exhibition Centre during the Apec Economic Leaders’ Meeting. Photo: Sam Tsang
Ma noted that Hong Kong’s role in Shenzhen’s development had evolved over the decades, from providing the largest source of foreign direct investment, through manufacturing facilities, property development and even subway construction, to becoming an initial public offering (IPO) destination for Shenzhen companies.
Official statistics show that of about 2,700 listed companies in Hong Kong, 174 originate from Shenzhen.
“Hong Kong’s status as an international financial centre has supported Shenzhen’s development,” Ma said, adding that the city’s hosting of the Apec finance ministers’ meeting in October underscored Beijing’s recognition of that stature.
People pose for photos from a Shenzhen overpass near the Langham Hotel, a property with Hong Kong ties, on November 18. Photo: Reuters
Hong Kong’s footprint in Shenzhen is visible across real estate, ports, factories and hospitality.
The five-star Langham Hotel in Futian district, where US President Donald Trump is staying during the leaders’ summit, is owned by Shenzhen East Pacific Group, which was founded by Hong Kong tycoon Bill Wong Cho-bau. The property is operated by Langham Hospitality, a unit of the Lo family’s Hong Kong-listed Great Eagle.
Ma noted that Kylin Villa, the state-owned lakeside resort used for high-profile sideline meetings – including talks between Chinese President Xi Jinping, Trump and their Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin – was built in 1997 by a former Hong Kong-listed company, Kumagai Gumi (Hong Kong), of which Ma was deputy chairman at the time.
In 1996, the company also built Shenzhen’s once-tallest skyscraper, the 69-storey “Diwang Building”. The name, which translates to “Land King” in English, came from the plot of land it sits on, which set a then-record auction price for land in the city.
“Superman” Li Ka-shing, founder of CK Hutchison, invested in Yantian Port through Hutchison Ports, which now operates the strategic asset in partnership with the Shenzhen municipal government.
An aerial view of the site earmarked for The Loop station in Hong Kong’s Northern Metropolis, presented to Apec delegates as a key cross-border growth driver. Photo: Karma Lo
Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu used the Apec meetings to present Hong Kong’s latest developments and strengths, including the Northern Metropolis megadevelopment, to seven of the 21 Apec economies – Malaysia, Vietnam, Brunei, Thailand, Chile, Peru and Singapore.
“As part of the Greater Bay Area, Hong Kong is the most open and international city in China and serves as a platform to facilitate the two-way flow of capital,” Lee told the media.
Some delegates said the summits underscored Hong Kong’s unique value and status at a time when geopolitical complexities were forcing a rapid restructuring of global trade.
“As companies look to diversify their supply chains and navigate new markets to mitigate risk, Hong Kong’s role as the ‘ultimate bridge’ becomes indispensable,” Hong Kong General Chamber of Commerce chairman Jacob Kam Chak-pui told the SCMP.
“We are uniquely positioned to turn these global complexities into tangible, cross-border commercial opportunities.”
Judith Yu, CEO and executive director of HKI China Land, said she used the gathering to highlight to delegates the advantages of Hong Kong, pointing to its common law system, free flow of capital and information, and strong professional services.
“Many delegates are seeing Shenzhen and Hong Kong directly like this for the first time … the two cities form the front and back ends of an industrial chain,” Yu said.
“[Foreign enterprises] focused on how to use Hong Kong as a base to enter the GBA,” she said, referring to the Greater Bay Area, which comprises Hong Kong, Macau and nine cities in Guangdong province.
“There is genuine interest in Hong Kong from the global business community.”
Wingco Lo Kam-wing, president of the Chinese Manufacturers’ Association of Hong Kong, told the SCMP that he had connected with mainland enterprises looking to expand overseas, and others planning to establish operations in Hong Kong after completing their company registrations.
He also forged ties with companies and chambers of commerce from South Korea and Thailand across sectors including logistics, commodities trading and manufacturing.
Describing the talks as just starting points that would need following up to yield deals, Lo said he had already arranged meetings in Hong Kong.
He also expressed confidence that the businesses would be keen to visit and participate in the technology-led Northern Metropolis development, although he noted that many were still unfamiliar with the megaproject.
Taking advantage of Shenzhen’s proximity, Irons Sze Wing-wai, executive director of Hang Tung Resources, invited delegates to make a side trip to Hong Kong to visit the Northern Metropolis, with many of them having only heard of the project.
“They can connect directly with government departments and local businesses,” Sze said.
“Such visits are far more convincing, and that is precisely the bonus opportunity that hosting Apec in Shenzhen has brought to Hong Kong.”
Sze also said summit discussions focused on building an inclusive AI ecosystem and deepening cross-border collaboration in computing power and applications, with the bay area offering a concrete model of that synergy.
“During the summit, I saw many local enterprises connecting with companies from Southeast Asia, North America and Oceania on green investment, R&D collaboration, cross-border financing and professional services, with numerous preliminary talks under way,” Sze added.
“For Hong Kong’s business community, the bigger takeaway is building long-term mutual trust … to facilitate sustained economic and trade cooperation between our country and Asia-Pacific economies.”
By Denise Tsang, Matthew Cheng

title_en: Trump says no rush to decide on new Iran strikes, looks to next year
content_en:
The president appears to be extending his timeline, after earlier suggesting Iran would be more amenable to a deal after the US midterms.
US President Donald Trump gestures as he boards Air Force One at Shenzhen Airport on Thursday. Photo: Reuters
US President Donald Trump on Thursday appeared to push a decision on renewed major strikes against Iran into next year, extending a timeline that he had previously suggested could come to a head after this month’s US midterm elections.
Asked in an interview about the possibility of new strikes, Trump said: “Well, I’ll talk to you about it after the beginning of the year.”
“We’ve got time,” ‌Trump added, speaking from his plane as he returned to Washington from his trip to China.
In recent weeks, Trump has alternated between threats of escalation against Iran and indicating he could wind down hostilities, with the two sides in a stand-off over efforts to resolve the conflict.
Trump gave a similar timeline in two other interviews.
“We’ll see what happens after January 1,” he told Fox News in an interview that aired on Thursday, while saying in a separate interview with a reporter for Axios and Israel’s News 12: “I’m not rushing to make any decisions on Iran.”
US Democratic Senators Tammy Duckworth (right) and Kirsten Gillibrand speak to reporters in Washington about a government funding amendment to defund the Iran war on Thursday. Photo: EPA
In the weeks leading up to the November 3 ⁠congressional contests, Trump repeatedly suggested that Iran would be more willing to strike a deal in the eight-month conflict following the US elections.
But after his fellow Republicans lost both ‌chambers of Congress, his administration last week said it believes its blockade and economic sanctions against Iran are working. The US Senate, which Republicans control until January 3, again on Thursday rejected a measure aimed at curbing the war.
Trump has acknowledged Iran played a ‌role in the losses but has said he would not have changed course.
US Vice-President J.D. Vance, a possible 2028 presidential candidate, publicly distanced himself ⁠from the war, which he blamed for ⁠the party’s political rout. Trump later directed Vance away from Iran diplomatic efforts to instead focus on domestic matters.
“J.D. was fine,” Trump said when asked about the vice-president’s social media post. “What he ‌said was right. He said that the whole situation is one of the reasons certainly that the election didn’t go our way.”
“And the big thing is if you had to do it again, would you do it? ‌And ‌the answer is yes. Because you can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon,” Trump said.
Thursday’s joint statement issued following Trump’s summit with his Russian and Chinese counterparts ‌did not mention the conflict with Iran.
US Vice-President J.D. Vance holds a knife at the 2nd Marine Aircraft Wing’s annual Marine Corps Birthday Ball in New Bern, North Carolina, on November 12. Photo: AP
Trump, on Fox News, was also asked about a report carried by CNN this week that Iran was planning to detonate ⁠a “dirty bomb” in Washington. A dirty bomb uses conventional explosives to spread radioactive material.
He appeared to downplay such a threat, saying, “I don’t think so,” when asked if people ⁠in the capital should be alarmed, although he also said there were indications Iran was “looking at” biological or chemical weapons, without elaborating.
“There is indication that Iran is looking at gases, looking at bio, because we’ve shut them out with the nuclear. Nuclear is much harder. And they’re looking at gas ‌and … biological weapons – not nice – and other things,” ‌Trump said.
Iran’s foreign ministry, in a post on social media, said US accusations about Tehran developing chemical and biological weapons were intended to create fear and justify military action. It earlier this week called the CNN report “baseless”.
Israel, the US and other Western countries have long accused Iran of seeking nuclear weapons, which Tehran denies. Destroying Iran’s nuclear programme was one of Trump’s main justifications when he launched strikes against Iran in February alongside Israel.
By Reuters

title_en: World-famous hippo Fiona dies in US days after swallowing visitor’s hat
content_en:
Vets tried several times to remove the woolly cap but were unable to save the animal, who was beloved for her antics on social media.
Fiona the hippo eats a specially made birthday cake to celebrate turning three in her enclosure at the Cincinnati Zoo in January 2020. Photo: AP
World-famous hippopotamus Fiona has died after several failed attempts by vets to remove a woolly hat that she accidentally swallowed, the Cincinnati Zoo announced Thursday.
Beloved for her antics on social media, the nine-year-old Nile hippo ingested the knitted cap last week and began to lose her appetite.
“It is with extreme sadness that we share with you the devastating news that Fiona did not make it after multiple attempts from our amazing vets and keeper team to help her through what ended up being a medical emergency,” the zoo wrote on social media.
“The vet staff tried everything they could to help her after she ingested a hat that ended up in her habitat by accident last week.
“Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome. The team performed necessary supportive care today in an attempt to save her, but it was not successful and she did not recover.”
Her plight triggered an outpouring of global support. “I have never prayed so much for a hippo to poop,” one social media user said.
A statue dedicated to Fiona the hippo sits outside the Cincinnati Zoo on Thursday. Photo: AP
Others blamed the parents of a child who, according to the zoo, threw a hat in the air, which was then caught by a ceiling fan and sent flying.
Fiona’s care team resorted to unusual methods, using a “vibration plate” borrowed from a local horse farm to “help encourage movement through her digestive tract and help the object pass”, the zoo said in a social media post.
They also offered her a sniff of coffee, to which she responded with approving grunts and ear twitches.
Mike Wenninger, the zoo’s director of animal health, said she had been under 24-hour supervision and medical care that included enemas and pain and anti-nausea medication.
Because she was full-grown, surgery was not considered a viable option, and attempts to retrieve the hat with a nine-foot-long (2.74-metre-long) scope, passed through her rectum while she was sedated, were unsuccessful.
Fiona was born in January 2017, the first Nile hippo born at the Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden in 75 years.
She was premature and initially unable to stand or nurse from her mother, Bibi, but staged a remarkable recovery.
Fiona and her younger brother Fritz, born in 2022, charmed people across the world with videos of them chomping on watermelons, wading through their water tanks surrounded by tilapia fish and reaching up for leaves.
The Cincinnati Zoo opened in 1875, making it the second-oldest zoo in the United States.
By Agence France-Presse

title_en: Innovation stagnation: why China keeps buying less from Europe amid overall import surge
content_en:
Meanwhile growth in East Asia’s exports to China could be somewhat of an aberration driven by the AI buildout, economists say.
Shipping containers are stacked at the Rhine-Neckar commercial port in Mannheim, Germany, on November 12. Photo: EPA
China’s imports grew faster than its exports in October, but while its East Asian neighbours benefited from the surge, Europe missed out.
The split in China’s latest trade figures partly reflected European industry’s long-time stagnation in traditional sectors, according to some analysts, who said innovation was the long-term way out of the continent’s trade imbalance with China.
Others cautioned that East Asian economies share some of the advantages Europe considered unfair, such as weak currencies, and that beneath the semiconductor boom, their industries were also under strain from Chinese competition.
Mainland China’s imports from Taiwan, South Korea and Japan rose 41.1 per cent, 110.2 per cent and 26.5 per cent year on year in October, respectively, according to the latest Chinese customs data. That left it with trade deficits of US$17.1 billion with Taiwan, US$13.6 billion with South Korea and, despite political tension, US$3.3 billion with Japan.
Europe did not share in the expansion. China’s imports from the EU fell 4.2 per cent, and its trade surplus with the bloc reached US$33.4 billion.
Overall, China’s imports rose 41.6 per cent from a year earlier, compared with 35.2 per cent for exports.
